Touring Together: The Two-Up Experience

Sharing a motorcycle tour with a pillion passenger transforms the experience from a solo adventure into a shared journey of discovery. But two-up touring requires more preparation, better bike setup, and different riding techniques than solo touring. Get it right and you create memories together. Get it wrong and you create arguments.

Communication Is Everything

A Bluetooth intercom system is the single most important piece of kit for pillion touring. Being able to talk to each other while riding eliminates the frustration of trying to communicate through taps and gestures. The pillion can alert the rider to hazards, request comfort stops, and share the enjoyment of the scenery in real time.

Riding Technique with a Pillion

  • Smoother inputs — Every throttle, brake, and steering input is amplified for the pillion. Smooth, progressive riding prevents the helmet-clash that happens when you brake suddenly.
  • Longer braking distances — The extra weight significantly increases stopping distances. Leave more room than you would solo.
  • Wider lines through corners — The additional weight changes your bike's turning dynamics. Use wider, more flowing lines rather than aggressive lean angles.
  • Slower manoeuvres — Low-speed riding is harder with a pillion. Practice U-turns and slow-speed manoeuvres in a car park before hitting the road.

Bike Setup for Two-Up

Increase rear preload to compensate for the pillion's weight. Adjust tyre pressures to the two-up specification in your owner's manual. Check the mirrors are adjusted for the slightly different riding position with a pillion. Ensure the pillion has proper grab handles or a grab strap.

Best Bikes for Pillion Touring

BMW R 1300 GS — The raised rear seat gives the pillion an excellent view over the rider's shoulders. Heated rear seat option is luxury. Electronic suspension adapts to two-up weight automatically.

Honda Gold Wing — The ultimate pillion machine with a throne-like rear seat, audio system, heated grips and seat, and armrest. No motorcycle carries a pillion more comfortably.

Kawasaki Versys 1000 SE — Smooth engine and comfortable rear seat. The suspension handles two-up weight well and the grab handles are well-positioned.

Triumph Tiger 1200 — Good pillion seat height and comfort. The triple engine delivers smooth, manageable power for two-up riding.

The pillion's comfort determines the tour's success. An uncomfortable passenger will want to stop every 45 minutes, turning a 300-mile day into a 200-mile ordeal. Invest in pillion comfort before your own — they cannot control the ride like you can.

Planning for Two

Allow for more frequent stops, reduce daily mileage targets by 20-30 percent, and choose accommodation with secure parking. Pack lighter — two people's gear fills luggage faster than you expect. Consider posting clothes ahead to hotels to reduce on-bike luggage.

faq.q: Do I need to change my bike setup for a pillion?
faq.a: Yes. Increase rear preload to compensate for the passenger's weight and restore correct ride height, and set tyre pressures to the two-up figure in your manual, usually a little higher at the rear. Check your mirrors suit the slightly changed riding position, and make sure the pillion has secure grab handles or a strap before setting off.

faq.q: How does a pillion change my riding?
faq.a: Every input is amplified for the passenger, so throttle, braking and steering must be smoother and more progressive to avoid helmet clash. The extra weight lengthens braking distances significantly and changes cornering dynamics, so use wider, flowing lines and leave more room. Low-speed manoeuvres are harder, so practise U-turns in a car park before a big trip.

faq.q: How do I keep my pillion comfortable on long days?
faq.a: Prioritise their comfort over your own because they cannot control the ride. Fit an intercom so they can request breaks, reduce daily mileage by 20 to 30 percent, and plan more frequent stops. Consider a seat cushion, a backrest and heated seat for their comfort. An uncomfortable pillion will want to stop every 45 minutes, turning a long day into an ordeal.

faq.q: What is the best bike for pillion touring?
faq.a: Bikes with an elevated, well-padded rear seat and good weather protection suit two-up touring best. The BMW R 1300 GS gives the pillion an excellent view, the Honda Gold Wing offers armchair comfort with heating and audio, and the Kawasaki Versys 1000 SE and Triumph Tiger 1200 both carry a passenger well. Take your pillion along to test-sit any bike before buying.
